newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn says would send peacekeeper troops to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Bonn says would send peacekeeper troops to Bosnia.

text.p: Germany, shedding some of its reluctance to send troops to Bosnia, said on Sunday it would be prepared to contribute infantry peacekeepers with armoured vehicles to a future mission.
But the Defence Ministry said that it would not send "combat troops" armed with heavy weapons like tanks and mortars.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said in a newspaper interview that Bonn will seek as normal a military role as possible if German troops take part in a future mission after the IFOR peacekeeping force's one-year mandate runs out in December.

A Defence Ministry spokesman said: "Defence Minister (Volker) Ruehe has outlined to parliament and the public a possible German military involvement in a still-to-be-decided new peacekeeping mandate ordered by United Nations and NATO.
"(This could include) the deployment of security and monitoring forces (infantry troops with armoured wheeled vehicles), with logistics and medical support."

The statement said any German force sent would have a "security and monitoring" role aimed at preventing any resurgence of war. The spokesman dismissed German newspaper reports these would be "combat troops".
German units currently provide medical and logistics support for the NATO-led IFOR peacekeeping IFOR in a region the Nazis occupied during much of World War Two.
This would have been unthinkable before German unification in 1990, when the country began to shed its post-war qualms about sending troops abroad on any mission.
Some NATO partners feel Germany should shoulder more of the burden of peace missions and German leaders have suggested that Germany should edge toward a full military role.
Kinkel told Welt am Sonntag that in a new mission "our partners would have little understanding for a special German (military) role".
IFOR's mandate runs out in December and it is still not certain that some form of security force will remain in Bosnia after IFOR pulls out.

Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe have said some kind of security force was needed until military equilibrium between the former warring parties had been established and that the force should include German troops.
Other NATO members have said little and Washington has refused to comment until after U.S. elections on November 5.
